problem_shape: This family is about making a designed experience survive contact with the body and the physical world. In ProXeek, the screen can show a virtual object, but the user's hand still meets an ordinary room. The problem is to make that room supply a believable touch target without custom machines or a prebuilt prop. In Mechanical Cloaking of Halftoned Imagery, the object must do two jobs at once: from the outside it should show a target picture made from pores, while mechanically it should behave like one plain material rather than a patterned weak-and-strong patchwork. The shared shape of the problem is cross-sense agreement. A visual design, a touch sensation, and a physical response all have to line up enough that the user or observer accepts the object. The papers are siblings because both refuse to treat appearance as separate from matter. They ask how to choose or design physical structure so it carries a second meaning: a room object can stand in for virtual touch, and a porous material can hide a picture inside a nearly uniform mechanical behavior.
naive_failure: A smart beginner would try to solve each sense separately. For virtual reality touch, they might 3D-print a replica, buy a force-feedback device, or let the user see the object without feeling it. That fails because replicas require preparation, active devices are bulky and expensive, and visual-only interaction leaves the hand with no matching evidence. For halftoned mechanical imagery, they might simply punch darker and lighter pore patterns to match a picture. That fails because the same holes that make the image also change how forces travel through the object. A dark region could become softer or directionally biased, so an outside mechanical test would reveal the hidden pattern. In both cases, the simple plan forgets that the body and material do not read labels. They respond to size, position, texture, stiffness, porosity, and direction of force all at once.
mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is constrained matching: choose a physical arrangement that satisfies several kinds of evidence at the same time. In ProXeek, the system starts with virtual objects annotated by designers with emphasized touch qualities. It also receives snapshots of the user's real environment from a commodity headset. The question is not merely which object has the right name. The chosen proxy must plausibly match touch qualities, fit the virtual object's role, and satisfy geometric limits such as where the object is and whether the user can use it. The system scores competing room objects against several goals, then selects viable proxies. In Mechanical Cloaking, the adjustable thing is a parametric porous structure, meaning a family of hole patterns controlled by settings. The structure must visually act like halftoning, where small light and dark marks combine into an image, while its averaged mechanical behavior remains close to uniform and direction-independent. What counts as wrong is concrete: poor visual contrast, a bad match to the target picture, or effective stiffness that changes with direction or location. The tradeoff is expressiveness versus concealment: enough visible variation to draw an image, but not enough mechanical variation to betray it.
why_math_matters: The math matters because these are not one-property objects. A room object in ProXeek is useful only through a bundle of relations: it has a shape, a material feel, a place in the room, and a possible correspondence to a virtual object. No single rule such as pick the nearest object can capture that bundle. The matching logic exploits the fact that real environments already contain many possible substitutes, and that language-and-image reasoning can connect descriptions like hardness, texture, and object purpose to visible room evidence. Mechanical Cloaking exploits a different structure: a porous material has two scales. Up close, holes form visible dots that can make a halftone image. From the viewpoint of a larger force test, many holes together can behave like an averaged material. If the pore family is chosen carefully, the visual pattern can vary while the averaged mechanical response stays nearly the same in all directions. In both papers, the math is bookkeeping for hidden coupling: changing what is seen also changes what is felt or how force passes through.
paper_family: ProXeek and Mechanical Cloaking look different on the surface, but both are about assigning physical things a second role without breaking their first role. ProXeek keeps the user's room as itself, then asks whether a pillow, cup, table, or other found object can also serve as a virtual touch proxy. Its central move is to compare designer-provided haptic intent with headset-captured room evidence, using multimodal reasoning and a multi-goal scoring process to find candidates that feel more convincing than visual-only interaction or generic printed replicas. Mechanical Cloaking starts with fabricated matter rather than a furnished room. It designs porous structures whose holes form a target image like a printed halftone, while numerical experiments show the structure can remain close to mechanically homogeneous and isotropic, meaning it responds almost like one uniform material and not like a directional pattern. One paper searches existing matter for a perceptual match; the other designs matter so perception and force response can coexist. The common deeper move is to treat perception as a constraint on physical structure, not as a surface decoration added after the real object is chosen.
what_changed: The 2026 version of this family seems to push multisensory graphics toward ordinary physical settings. ProXeek does not assume a special haptic lab; it uses commodity headset snapshots and objects already in the user's environment. Mechanical Cloaking does not treat a picture as only ink or pixels; it asks whether the visual image can be embedded into load-bearing porous structure while hiding its mechanical trace. The shift is from adding separate sensory hardware or decorative appearance toward making physical context do more work. These papers also show a stronger concern for competing requirements: touch match versus availability and geometry in ProXeek, visual contrast versus uniform mechanical behavior in Mechanical Cloaking.
limits: The evidence is narrow. ProXeek depends on designer annotations, headset snapshots, available room objects, and the reasoning system's ability to infer touch-relevant properties from visual and language evidence. A room with poor substitutes, unsafe layouts, hidden object properties, or unusual virtual interactions could break the match, and the user study does not prove every home or application will work. Mechanical Cloaking depends on the chosen class of porous structures and numerical experiments; the abstract does not prove that any target image, material, scale, or manufacturing process will preserve near-uniform mechanical behavior. Both papers also rely on perception thresholds: the touch proxy or cloaked material only has to be convincing enough under the tested conditions, not physically identical to the thing it represents.
